defaults.teacher_persona: A database-minded analyst who insists the question is written in plain English before it becomes SQL, and who predicts the row count of a query before running it.
classmates: A spreadsheet user moving to a real database who expects a formula and gets a join
An analyst who writes queries that work but cannot say what a NULL did to the result
defaults.interaction: Predict-then-run: the classmates write the English question, predict the shape and row count of the result, write the SQL, and reconcile the difference when they are wrong.
defaults.assessment: Each classroom ends with 3-5 checks aligned to the chapter's graded activity.

classrooms.title: Tables, Keys, and Relationships
classrooms.prompt: Introduce the relational model on a small schema — customers, orders, order lines — and have the classmates identify primary keys, foreign keys, and where a one-to-many becomes a many-to-many. Then ask for one question the schema cannot answer, and why.
objectives: Read a schema and identify keys and relationships
Explain what a foreign key enforces
Tell when a question needs a table the schema does not have

activities.title: Read the schema, name the keys

classrooms.title: SELECT Reads; Everything Else Narrows
classrooms.prompt: Walk the shape of a query — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT — and have the classmates fix three broken queries: one selecting the wrong column, one filtering with a string against a number, and one where NULL quietly removes rows. Predict the row count before running each fix.
objectives: Write a filtered, ordered query from a plain-English question
Explain how WHERE treats NULL and why the result was smaller than expected
Use LIMIT deliberately rather than to hide a wrong filter

classrooms.title: Collapse Many Rows, Combine Tables
classrooms.prompt: Take the two ideas that do real reporting work: aggregates with GROUP BY and joins across a shared key. Have the classmates build a monthly revenue report by joining orders to customers, then compare an inner and a left join on the same query and explain the rows that appeared or vanished.
objectives: Summarise a table with COUNT, SUM, and AVG per group
Join two tables on their key and know which rows survive
Choose between inner, left, and full joins for a reporting question

activities.title: Where did those rows go? inner vs left

classrooms.title: Creating and Changing Data Safely
classrooms.prompt: Move from reading to writing: CREATE TABLE with types, keys, and constraints, then ALTER and DML. Give the classmates a change request against a live-looking table and have them write it so that a bad row cannot get in — including the transaction they would wrap it in and the row count they would check afterwards.
objectives: Define a table with the constraints that keep bad rows out
Change a schema or its data without losing what was there
Wrap a write in a transaction and verify the effect by count
